book: 308 - The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy

chapters.file: ch94 - 88. Watchmen as Philosophy Illustrating Time and Free Will.md
chapters.relation: Goldberg and Gavaler argue that Moore and Gibbons's Watchmen operationalizes eternalism (McTaggart's B-series) both through its rigid 3x3 grid and mirror-symmetric layouts and through Doctor Manhattan, who narrates all moments as simultaneously present ('nothing ever ends'). Because eternalism means no one could have done otherwise, libertarian free will is ruled out, and the chapter argues the operative view is compatibilism rather than determinism, using Frankfurt's rejection of the principle of alternative possibilities and Dennett's Luther example to read Doctor Manhattan's hesitant killing of Rorschach as free action he could not have done otherwise.

chapters.file: ch95 - 89. The Joker as Philosopher Killing Jokes.md
chapters.relation: Brake reads Moore and Bolland's The Killing Joke as staging Camus's absurd: the Joker tortures Commissioner Gordon to prove the world is random and unjust ('one bad day') and that reason, tied to continuous memory, should be abandoned for a fragmented 'multiple choice' self. Drawing on Nietzsche's wave-like unstable self (via Morrison's 'super-sane' Joker) and Foucault on how madness haunts modern reason, the chapter argues Batman and Gordon also flirt with madness, while questioning whether the Joker, seeking revenge, has really embraced the absurd or is more rational than he admits.

chapters.file: ch96 - 90. From Hell as Philosophy Ripping Through Structural Violence.md
chapters.relation: James and Mona Rocha argue that Moore and Campbell's From Hell links physical and structural violence under patriarchy: William Gull's Ripper murders of Whitechapel sex workers, and his premonition of the dull modern office ('the twentieth century, I have delivered it'), show how sensationalized physical violence pushes routine structural violence into the invisible background where it corrupts men morally (Gull and Abberline both lose their humanity). Using Galtung's structural violence and Crenshaw's intersectionality of poverty and gender, plus the male gaze in Gull's ghostly viewing of female workers, the chapter connects Victorian misogyny to present-day workplace sexual harassment.

chapters.file: ch97 - 91. Deadpool’s Killogy as Philosophy The Metaphysics of a Homicidal Journey Through Possible Worlds.md
chapters.relation: Manninen argues that Cullen Bunn's Deadpool 'Killogy' is best read through David Lewis's genuine modal realism and counterpart theory: when Deadpool enters the Nexus of All Realities and finds piles of distinct Spider-Man corpses, he discovers other worlds are concrete and their inhabitants are counterparts, not identical selves, refuting Plantinga's actualist transworld identity. Framing Deadpool as an anti-Sisyphean 'hero' who tries to end the Absurd (the Continuity) by killing everyone rather than affirming it as Camus's Sisyphus does, the chapter supplements Lewis with Thomasson's artifact theory of fiction to handle the literary characters of the Ideaverse.

chapters.file: ch98 - 92. V for Vendetta as Philosophy Victory Through the Virtues of Anarchy.md
chapters.relation: Nisley argues that Moore and Lloyd's V for Vendetta justifies V's violent rebellion against the Norsefire regime through Locke: the fascist state seized power without consent, tortured and experimented on citizens (V at Larkhill), and violated natural rights, thereby placing itself in a state of war so the people may overthrow it. Using Aristotle on deviant constitutions and the beast-like tyrant (Adam Susan) who lacks practical wisdom, and contrasting Locke's tolerable state of nature with Hobbes's brutal one, the chapter concludes the citizens should rebuild a rights-protecting social contract rather than V's leaderless anarchy, and maps the argument onto real-world 2020 events (BLM riots vs. the Whitmer kidnapping plot).

chapters.file: ch99 - 93. Asterios Polyp as Philosophy Master of Two Worlds.md
chapters.relation: Richards reads Mazzucchelli's Asterios Polyp as a visual meditation on universals versus particulars and the abstract versus concrete, using its CMYK color coding and character styles (Asterios as cool geometric solids, Hana as warm crosshatching) to stage Plato's two worlds. Asterios, a 'paper architect' living in perfect uninstantiated abstraction, undergoes an inverted Hero's Journey (Campbell's monomyth) down into the concrete world—building an actual treehouse, telling the Ise shrine story—to become 'master of two worlds,' reconciling Form and matter, universal and particular, and accepting impermanence just as an asteroid closes on Earth.

chapters.file: ch100 - 94. Yes, Roya and Philosophy The Art of Submission.md
chapters.relation: Goldberg, Gavaler, and Chavez use Trotman and Denich's Yes, Roya—where Roya dominates Joe and Wylie professionally (publishing under Joe's name) and sexually, all consensually—to ask how the three major Western ethical theories can accommodate consensual dominant/submissive relationships. They argue Aristotle's virtue ethics handles them via unequal friendships (submissives depending more, within a mean), Kant's Formula of Universal Law permits them once consent is built into the maxim (aligning with the Formula of Humanity), and Mill's utilitarianism sanctions them because justice and felt safety, grounded in consent, follow from the Greatest Happiness Principle.

chapters.file: ch101 - 95. The Walking Dead as Philosophy Rick Grimes and Community Building in an Apocalypse.md
chapters.relation: Jones argues that Kirkman's The Walking Dead uses Rick Grimes's community-building to probe utopia and dystopia, reading the prison, Alexandria, Woodbury, the Saviors, and the Commonwealth through Aristotle's six constitutional forms—with the polity (rule by many for the common good enabling eudaimonia) as the standard for a good society and tyranny/oligarchy/corrupt forms marking dystopias like Negan's compound and the class-tyrannical Commonwealth. Invoking More's and Mill's coinages of utopia and dystopia, the chapter asks why Rick's final society, despite his moral evolution, ends up rebuilding the hierarchical pre-apocalyptic order rather than the more egalitarian, flourishing alliance he had forged.

holes.name: Structural Violence
holes.what: Johan Galtung's concept that unjust social structures inflict harm and unequal life chances without a direct physical perpetrator.
holes.why: Chapter 96's entire thesis is that From Hell connects physical violence to structural violence under patriarchy, and no taxonomy concept names this central idea.

holes.name: Counterpart Theory
holes.what: David Lewis's view that a thing's modal properties are grounded in similar-but-nonidentical counterparts existing in other concrete possible worlds, not in transworld identity.
holes.why: Chapter 97 argues Deadpool's piles of distinct hero corpses can only be understood via Lewis's counterpart relation as a substitute for identity; possible-worlds alone does not capture the counterpart/transworld-identity distinction the chapter turns on.

holes.name: The Hero's Journey (Monomyth)
holes.what: Joseph Campbell's archetypal narrative structure of departure, initiation, and return through which a hero is transformed.
holes.why: Chapter 99 structures its whole reading of Asterios Polyp around Campbell's monomyth (its 17 stages), an organizing framework with no counterpart in the taxonomy.
